title: Sue Cleaver hails Victoria Wood legacy as she joins Dinnerladies stage tour

input.lead: The stage adaptation of Victoria Wood's beloved sitcom will have a run at the Manchester Opera House
input.summary: The stage adaptation of Victoria Wood's beloved sitcom will have a run at the Manchester Opera House
input.evidence_text: Sue Cleaver hails Victoria Wood legacy as she joins Dinnerladies stage tour - BBC News Image caption, Victoria Wood wrote and played Brenda, the deputy canteen manager, in the BBC TV comedy show Dinnerladies Published 1 hour ago Actress Sue Cleaver has said Victoria Wood would be "over the moon" with a new stage adaptation of beloved sitcom Dinnerladies, which she hailed as "a celebration of her legacy". Best known as Eileen Grimshaw in ITV soap Coronation Street, Cleaver is among the famous faces joining the new production, which is the first to be commissioned by Wood's estate since her death in 2016 at the age of 62. The 63-year-old, who featured in the BBC show as a recurring character, will take the stage as cynical canteen worker Jean, who was played by Anne Reid in the show. She said the script it "blew her away" and that it had been "beautifully adapted" from Wood's show. The show, created, written and co-produced by Wood, aired on the BBC from 1998 to 2000 and followed the workplace dramas of the staff and regulars in a canteen at a factory in Manchester. More than 25 years on, Cleaver told BBC Radio Manchester the sitcom, which ran for two series was "observational comedy at its finest". She said: "I'm thrilled to be doing it. "It's such a celebration of Vic's work. It's about the celebration of her and her legacy. "I think she'd be over the moon and I'm very excited to be a part of it." Cleaver added: "There's no way [the audience] are not going to be able to enjoy this show. "It's a British classic and nobody writes the way Vic writes. "If you've never been in a theatre in your life, make this the one time that you do come because it won't let you down." title: Murdered children 'petrified' by attacks on home, inquest hears

input.lead: Michelle Pearson and her four children were murdered in an arson attack at their home in Walkden
input.summary: Michelle Pearson and her four children were murdered in an arson attack at their home in Walkden
input.evidence_text: Murdered children 'petrified' by attacks on home, inquest hears - BBC News Image source, Family photos Image caption, The four Pearson children died during the petrol bomb attack, and their mother died 20 months later. By Phil Cunliffe Reporting from Bolton Coroners' Court Published 5 October 2026 Four children had been "petrified" by a series of attacks on their home before a petrol bomb attack killed them all, an inquest has heard. Demi Pearson, 15, her brother Brandon, eight, and sisters Lacie, seven, Lia, three, died at their home in Jackson Street in Walkden in Greater Manchester in December 2017. Their mother Michelle, 37, was badly burned and died in August 2019. The inquest at Bolton Coroner's Court - scheduled to last eight weeks - heard that Michelle had told police she did not feel safe in the house, which had been covered in graffiti and had its windows smashed. Zak Bolland and David Worrall were jailed for life in 2018 for the murder of the four children, and in 2021 also convicted of Michelle's murder. Bolland was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum of 40 years and Worrall was sentenced to life with a minimum of 37 years in jail. Two weeks before the fatal attack, Bolland smashed windows at the house with a hammer, leaving glass everywhere. In a statement read out to the inquest, relatives said Michelle was traumatised and the called police on five separate occasions. Her son Kyle – who escaped the blaze – said in a statement to the inquest that "the police didn't do anything". Image source, GMP Image caption, Michelle Pearson and her four children were murdered after an arson attack at their home in Walkden Michelle suffered 68% burns to her body and "clung on to life" until she died on August 25, 2019, around 20 months after the attack. input.summary: Manchester illustrator Stan Chow says he was not asked permission for use of his cartoon

title: BT agrees rescue deal to buy broadband operator TalkTalk

input.lead: BT's planned takeover of broadband operator TalkTalk is subject to regulator approval
input.summary: BT's planned takeover of broadband operator TalkTalk is subject to regulator approval
input.evidence_text: The takeover would end of months of speculation over the future of TalkTalk and mean services for its millions of customers will continue as normal BT boss Alison Kirkby said it provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers. The administrator, Alvarez & Marsal, said it also provided certainty for TalkTalk's 900 staff based in Salford, Greater Manchester However, Virgin Media called it a "stitch-up" which allows BT to "tighten its grip" over the market. The government has given itself the power to have the final say on the deal, citing its importance to vital public services TalkTalk has 1.5 million retail customers and one million wholesale customers across the UK BT's Kirkby told the BBC's Today programme: "Two and a half million customers, including vulnerable households, and key emergency services might have lost their services if Talk Talk had failed, which it was on track to do "So BT stepped in as we were the only viable option to take the business forward."

title: Man City TV presenter Natalie Pike's 'terrifying' stalker ordeal

input.lead: The Manchester City pundit said her stalker appeared at Etihad Stadium where she was working
input.summary: The Manchester City pundit said her stalker appeared at Etihad Stadium where she was working
input.evidence_text: Man City TV presenter Natalie Pike's 'terrifying' stalker ordeal - BBC News Image caption, Natalie Pike described her ordeal as "crazy" and "terrifying" By Stewart Whittingham North West Published 5 October 2026 A football presenter has described a "terrifying" eight-month ordeal in which her stalker turned up at a Premier League match where she was working. Former BBC Radio Manchester presenter Natalie Pike said the man was arrested after she recognised him while she was broadcasting at Etihad Stadium before Manchester City played Newcastle United in February. Ms Pike, who covered Scotland during the World Cup in the United States this summer, now works as City's in-house presenter as well as on other channels. Her stalker was last week given a suspended prison sentence and issued with a restraining order. Ms Pike said she had been on a spa day when her hairdresser called and said two men had come in trying to find her home address in the Cheshire village where she lives. The 43-year-old said she trawled through her Instagram messages and was able to identify one of the men. A week later, Ms Pike saw him again while she was on the pitch at Etihad Stadium. She said he was arrested the following day. He was convicted of stalking on 25 September and, in addition to the 12-month prison sentence suspended for 18 months and restraining order, was told he must carry out rehabilitation activity and do 100 hours' community service. The BBC has agreed to Ms Pike's request not to name him. Image source, PA Media Image caption, Natalie Pike works for Manchester City She told BBC Breakfast: "It has been terrifying for the last eight months not knowing what is happening or what he might do, for my safety but also my son's safety. "It has caused extreme anxiety for my whole family. "

title: 'It started with a cup of tea - now we help thousands'

input.lead: Twenty-five years ago Victoria "put a kettle on" for her community.
input.summary: Twenty-five years ago Victoria "put a kettle on" for her community. Now she helps more than 2,000 people
input.evidence_text: When Victoria Armstrong moved to Manchester as a university student in the 1990s she started to notice there were people living in her community who "had no-one" "I spent the first six months just putting on a kettle and putting bread in the toaster," the 53-year-old said Victoria, originally from Oxford, who had moved to Gorton after enrolling as a Fine Art student at Manchester University, started to host people for a cup of tea at her local church once a week Later she made it an official charity, founding Oasis in 2001 "It started with cups of tea and toast," Victoria said. "Twenty-five years later and we have helped thousands of people." Oasis now has its own centre, with 19 staff and 90 volunteers, running education classes, a free cafe, crisis support services, job clubs and a charity shop

title: Train station returning to Cheadle after more than 100 years

input.lead: Cheadle in Stockport has been without a train station since its original hub closed in 1917
input.summary: Cheadle in Stockport has been without a train station since its original hub closed in 1917
input.evidence_text: Work is beginning on bringing a train station back to the heart of a Greater Manchester village more than a century after its original station closed Cheadle in Stockport had a station just off the high street up until 1917 Funding for a new hub, which would be built next to Alexandra Hospital, was given the green light in 2022, with planning permission granted in 2023 but concerns about its effect on the timetabling of trains elsewhere on the network led to delays Stockport Council said the issue had now been resolved and council leader Mark Roberts said it was "a hugely significant moment for Cheadle and for Stockport" "For years we've fought for this station because we know the difference it will make to residents, businesses and the future prosperity of the area," he added Roberts said he was delighted that the initial highways work could now start on site thanks to the persistence and partnership of all involved

Credit: ITV News Reform UK and Labour have gone through to the second round of voting in the Greater Manchester Mayoral by-ele Neither Labour's Bev Craig or Reform UK's Sian Astley managed to secure a majority, meaning voters second choice ballots will now be counted to decide an overall winner Five candidates have now been eliminated from the contest to become Greater Manchester mayor – Geraldine Coggins (Green), Phil Eckersley (Conservative), Marcus Farmer (Independent), Richard Kilpatrick (Liberal Democrats) and Marlon West (Restore Britain) The by-election is using a voting system called supplementary vote (SV), which sees voters mark their ballot papers with a first and second choice, and if any candidate wins more than 50% of the first-choice votes, they are declared the winner That has not happened in Greater Manchester, so the top two candidates, Labour’s Bev Craig and Reform UK candidate Sian Astley, move to a second round ITV Granada Reports' Political Correspondent Lise McNally sent the latest from the Co-op Live as counting for the second round got underway

When I get there, the men are working in silence, hands sheathed in black gloves, bags of sweetcorn torn open, cardboard Just as I’m about to approach a vendor, I’m forwarded an email from a reader. Figures published by the TaxPayers’ Alliance put the annual total for the constituency at £130,714,966 in 2025/26 – equivalent to around £358,000 a day or £1,280 for every resident. The campaign group's new My Benefits Bill tool says the total has increased by 18.1% in two years. More than half of the £130.7m is accounted for by Universal Credit, with £68.2m spent in Altrincham and Sale West and 5,630 households claiming the benefit. A further £33.6m is spent on Personal Independence Payment (PIP), which helps people with the additional costs associated with long-term physical or mental health conditions or disabilities. There are 4,477 PIP claimants in the constituency. The remaining total comprises £10.7m in Housing Benefit, £9m in Disability Living Allowance, £5.4m in Employment and Support Allowance and £3.8m in Carer's Allowance. The figures should not be interpreted as showing that everyone receiving the benefits is unemployed. Universal Credit can be paid to people in work, while PIP is not means-tested and can be claimed regardless of whether someone is working. input.evidence_text: Town centre travel changes on the way – Bolton Council Published: Monday, 5th Oct 2026 Work is set to start on high quality, safe and attractive walking and cycling improvements in Bolton town centre, after Bolton Council secured over £5m of funding. The major upgrades aim to make every-day journeys simpler and more enjoyable and add to the ongoing regeneration of the town centre. Phase one of the scheme will focus on Bradshawgate and Great Moor Street. Roads will be resurfaced and footpaths repaved to make them more attractive and benefit people travelling on foot. There will be changes at side roads to give pedestrians priority, along with an upgraded pedestrian crossing on Bradshawgate near Nelson Square. Four junctions will be upgraded to make it easier and safer for people on foot and riding bikes to travel around the town centre. Segregated cycle paths will create safer routes for people of all ages and are especially valuable for younger or less confident riders, who may not feel comfortable mixing with traffic. Throughout construction, traffic management will be in place to keep the public and workers safe, with disruption kept to a minimum. Funding was first granted in 2023 from the Greater Manchester Mayor’s Cycling and Walking Challenge Fund and the council carried out extensive consultation that helped shape the plans. But work was delayed by the need to prepare for the demolition and regeneration of Crompton Place. With the removal of Crompton Place now underway, work on the travel improvements can get underway and construction is scheduled to begin on October 12. From a childhood in exile to surviving secret detention in China, his remarkable life and career have led him to global prominence. Using sculpture, installation, film, photography In Button Up! , the artist turns his lens on two centuries of Chinese and British relations. title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. title: Bolton Car Boot Sale

input.lead: Bolton Car Boot Sale at Bolton Car Boot Sale
input.summary: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and t
input.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and thousands of bargain hunters each week. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained.
